1: Chapter 1: A Visitor in the Rain
It had been raining on Pierrefeu for three days. In the spring, Claire Martin's elder sister had left for Paris, and since then Claire had been running the village's little pharmacy on her own.
When night fell, she closed the shutters, counted the day's takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when someone pounded violently on the door downstairs. A man's voice called out: "Is anyone there?"

On the doorstep stood a young man soaked to the bone, his left arm bound tight in a cloth stained with blood. He introduced himself: his name was Pierre Lapin, and he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"You have to treat me," Lapin said in a low voice. "I can pay. Three thousand five hundred francs—will that be enough?"
From inside his jacket he drew out a letter wrapped in oiled paper. "This letter must reach the abbey of Saint-Vent before the eighteenth of May."
Since her sister's departure, Claire had often felt blue in the evenings, but that night she had no time to dwell on it.
Yet she refused his money and said only: "At dawn tomorrow, I will take you up into the mountains."
2: At daybreak, they set out. Claire carried a basket on her back with bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the slope, they met old Gaston Roux, who was splitting wood. He set down his axe and told them in a low voice that the evening before, three strangers had been questioning people at the entrance to the village about a wounded young man.
"Take the footpath, my dear Claire," said Gaston Roux. "The main road isn't safe." Claire thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Claire walked ahead, placing each step with confidence. Lapin followed her without a word.
At noon the rain stopped; the mist slowly lifted, and the roof of the abbey of Saint-Vent appeared in the distance. At the gate stood a nun, Sister Agnès, whose task it was to welcome visitors.
Sister Agnès took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The Mother Abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years."
Lapin said to Claire, "I owe you my life." Claire smiled. "Then next time, fix the roof of my pharmacy." Lapin stayed at the abbey.
In the evening, Claire went back down the mountain alone. When she reached home, it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
